replacements.Trust by Construction:: Trust by Construction for Secure Agentic Workflows in Learning Institutions
replacements.Scale Intelligence Without: An executable reference for bounded authority and failure recovery
replacements.Agentic AI can access: Agentic AI can retrieve records, retain memory, delegate work and initiate institutional actions. Prompt injection and unreliable model behavior can turn those capabilities into unauthorized disclosure or change. Trust by Construction presents an executable reference architecture that constrains consequential actions independently of model intent. Its contribution is the composition of scoped authority, lineage-preserving memory, independent approval, revocation, bounded delivery and failure recovery. Synthetic cross-sector experiments contain 180 of 180 hostile scenarios and complete 58 of 58 benign tasks within declared interfaces. The reference also exercises real TLS handshakes against a controlled peer, tool-definition drift, monitor-induced restriction, remote-effect uncertainty and evidence-gated promotion. This revision adds developer-facing artifact retrieval that checks an independently approved digest before returning bytes, isolates concurrent response buffers, and prevents pending or malformed provider acknowledgements from becoming confirmed effects. It also addresses a channel that exact-byte release does not close: the information an agent carries in choices it is authorised to make. Canonicalising the destination, path, schedule and size of a release, then charging what remains against a per-task budget, reduces a measured sixteen-bit leak through authorised choices to one bit, and to zero when the release count is fixed with indistinguishable cover, while an ordinary workflow still completes. The repository supplies an offline example, regression tests, reproducible manuscript construction and explicit claim-to-evidence bindings. These results concern local controls and synthetic workflows; they do not establish model alignment, institutional utility or production security. Host isolation must still be supplied and tested in the intended deployment, live-model evaluation remains separate, and transport evidence from the loopback harness cannot qualify a production peer. The artifact supports engineering and teaching by making authority boundaries, failure outcomes and remaining obligations inspectable.
replacements.A reviewer of the previous revision made: The architecture requires the model runtime to reach protected services only through mediation. Isolation probes make that deployment assumption inspectable; they do not implement it. Seven required properties and one advisory property cover control-store permissions, process identity, enforcement-package integrity, metadata-service reachability, service-account tokens, a declared egress canary, standing credentials and kernel confinement. Each returns satisfied, violated or not measurable; not measurable is never counted as success. Qualification requires every mandatory measurement, the evidence is less than a day old, and it names an operator and a host. The repository host is expected to report reference; a test exists whose only purpose is to fail if they ever stop doing so. A cooperative probe is not an adversarial sandbox-escape evaluation, so deployment acceptance still requires testing a hostile process under the intended isolation policy.

developer_transport: Developer integration must distinguish peer identity from artifact identity. Silent Egress shows how outbound requests can disclose context even when a final answer appears harmless [12]; its results motivate observing network effects rather than inspecting answers alone. The v14 fetch_artifact API returns bytes only after matching an independently approved SHA-256 digest. A valid certificate and pinned key therefore do not authorize changed content. Each transfer keeps its response buffer local, preventing concurrent fetches from mixing bytes. Tests use real loopback TLS handshakes to check exact-byte success, changed-content rejection, concurrent transfers and malformed HTTP framing. The adapter is GET-only and sends no caller-supplied headers, cookies or request body. The caller must enforce the provenance and confidentiality of the requested path: an allowed path can itself carry sensitive data. This is not a general exfiltration detector or a firewall.
developer_recovery: Remote settlement also requires explicit evidence. Pending or malformed provider responses remain uncertain and continue to block dependent work; only an applied acknowledgement or authoritative terminal absence can settle the effect. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is rejected. Provider adapters must map asynchronous acceptance to pending, not applied, and must not interpret an eventually consistent missing record as terminal absence. The executable developer example follows a lost acknowledgement through pending lookup to confirmed reconciliation with one submission. These controls prevent false local confirmation under the tested responses; correctness still depends on the provider adapter honoring this contract. The ledger is a trusted integration component, not a model-facing authorization endpoint.
residual_channel: A fourth question follows from the third, and this revision is the first to answer it with a measurement. Release escrow fixes the bytes that leave, so a workload cannot put a student record into an approved artifact. It does not fix the decisions *around* those bytes. An agent holding entirely legitimate, repeated release authority still selects which approved destination receives a report, which approved path it lands on, when it is sent, and how large it is. None of these is an unauthorised act; each is a choice the system handed the model, and a choice is a channel. The 2026 implicit-injection results make the concern concrete rather than theoretical [12]: eight approved destinations are three bits per release, and an enrolment status is not many bits. The architecture therefore treats residual choice as an engineering quantity. Where the task contract can supply a value, it does, and the dimension carries nothing because the model never chose it; emission runs on a fixed schedule and artifact sizes are padded to declared buckets, which narrows timing and size the same way. What genuinely remains is counted in bits, charged against a declared per-task budget, and when the budget is spent the next release requires a named human rather than failing silently.
residual_channel_measurement: The bound is measured rather than asserted. An adversarial encoder that performs no unauthorised operation attempts to move a sixteen-bit secret through these choices, once for each of the 65,536 possible secrets, and the measurement counts how many distinct traces an external observer could distinguish. With every dimension left to the workload the secret crosses intact at 16.0 bits. Canonicalising destination, path, schedule and size reduces it to 1.0 bit, which is the residual carried by how many times the workload releases at all. Fixing the release count and padding with cover emissions that an observer cannot separate from real ones reduces it to 0.0 bits, a single observable trace for every secret. An ordinary two-release workflow completes under all three policies, so the reduction is not obtained by refusing to work; the cost appears instead as 98.4 per cent of adversarial tasks escalating to a named human, which is reported rather than omitted. The figures are an upper bound that assumes a perfect observer and an optimal decoder, they describe one encoder against this interface, and they say nothing about a channel outside the mediated release path. The measurement regenerates offline into audit/covert-channels.json and is checked by make all.
